standard.title: Recommended Practice for Building-Up by Thermal Spraying (First Revision)
standard.description: This standard covers recommendations for building-up worn or undersized surfaces using thermal spraying processes, including flame spray, high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF), wire arc spray, and plasma spray, as well as their related consumables (wire, powder, and gases).
standard.scope: This standard covers recommendations for building-up worn or undersized surfaces using thermal spraying processes, including flame spray, high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF), wire arc spray, and plasma spray, as well as their related consumables (wire, powder, and gases).

certification.description: Voluntary Engineering Code of Practice. Since IS 3023:2013 is an engineering guideline rather than a direct manufacturing product, it does not carry a separate mandatory BIS license or ISI certification mark. However, its design recommendations, process steps, undercutting depths, surface preparation, grit blasting, and finishing protocols are widely specified in public and private sector heavy engineering, thermal power plants, petrochemical facilities, machinery maintenance, and industrial repair procurement contracts to rebuild worn-out shafts and machinery components. Precious metal hallmarking is completely inapplicable.
requirements: Rebuilds worn components utilizing four main thermal spraying processes: flame spray, high velocity oxy-fuel (HVOF), wire arc spray, and plasma spray. Consumables like wire, powder feedstock, and carrier/fuel gases are fully co-regulated.

Machining or grinding away some of the good substrate material as well as the damaged surface to provide an adequate and uniform flat surface to accept the new thermal spray deposit. The ends of the undercut zone must be angled at 15° to 45° to the base metal (as shown in Fig. 1) to prevent notch effects or stress concentration.

Prior to roughening, all traces of oil, grease, paint, or other foreign contaminants must be completely removed from the undercut and adjacent surfaces. The undercut section must be roughened (such as by grit blasting) to ensure robust mechanical interlocking of the sprayed coating with the substrate.

Due to the low heat of combustion and low particle velocities of flame spray (both wire and powder) processes, both grit blasting and the application of an intermediate bond coating are usually required to ensure adequate bond strength.
For plasma spray processes, both surface roughening (via grit blasting) and the application of an intermediate bond coating are mandatory and essential to secure the coating.

Verification and certification of coating equipment must be performed either through regular calibration of process meters and pressure/flow gauges, or through demonstration of physical coating application, or a combination of both.

The effectiveness of the thermal spray coating depends heavily on final finishing. Finer grit grinding wheels must be used on dense, hard-to-penetrate coatings. Crucially, the coating must always be kept under compression during machining; grinding/cutting down through the sprayed surface towards the substrate minimizes delamination and particle pull-out.

Inspection must be performed after all finishing operations are complete. Both destructive (e.g. cross-section evaluation) and non-destructive (e.g. dye penetrant or ultrasonic) methods of evaluation may be utilized to verify bond integrity and thickness.
